tech.why_this_paper: Forces engineering leaders using LLM API relays/gateways to treat shared upstream credentials as a prompt-cache isolation failure mode, not a billing convenience.
tech.decision_it_changes: Whether to keep shared provider credentials/namespaces on the relay path, and what identity-preserving cache contract must be required of vendors/internal gateways.
tech.action_for_reader: This quarter: inventory every LLM relay/gateway in production; for each, document whether provider credentials/namespaces are shared across customers or tenants; run a cache-timing isolation probe on one non-prod path; require an identity-preserving cache contract in the next vendor/security review.
tech.talking_point: If your LLM relay maps many customers onto one provider cache identity, prompt-cache isolation can collapse even when customer auth looks separate.
tech.caveat: Evidence covers five open-source gateways, two providers, and a bounded production sample; prevalence on proprietary relays and full token-recovery impact are less certain.
tech.why_not_runner_up: Clearer immediate enterprise architecture decision and a concrete defense contract than the multi-agent collaboration-tax analysis, which is important but more diagnostic of agent design trade-offs than of a security control you can require this quarter.
tech.title: KeyPooling: Measuring Where LLM API Relay Paths Collapse Prompt Cache Isolation
tech.so_what: It demonstrates that shared relay credentials can collapse prompt-cache isolation across customers and provides a concrete identity-preserving defense contract with modest modeled cost.
tech.reason_not_higher: The measurements cover five open-source gateways, two providers, and a bounded production sample; prevalence across proprietary relay implementations and the full practical impact of token recovery remain less certain.

tech_runner_up.why_this_paper: Quantifies the hidden performance cost of making LLMs coordinate as a multi-agent team versus acting alone—useful when teams are defaulting to multi-agent architectures.
tech_runner_up.decision_it_changes: Whether a proposed multi-agent design is worth the coordination overhead for tasks that a single agent could already handle.
tech_runner_up.action_for_reader: Pick one production multi-agent workflow; measure end-to-end quality/cost against a strong single-agent baseline on the same task set; only keep multi-agent if the gain exceeds the measured collaboration tax.
tech_runner_up.talking_point: Multi-agent LLM systems can lose performance to coordination itself; the collaboration tax should be measured, not assumed away.
tech_runner_up.caveat: Framework is framed around two-player cooperative settings and solo-tractable tasks; larger topologies may behave differently.
tech_runner_up.title: The Collaboration Tax: How Much LLM Multi-Agent Systems Pay to Coordinate
tech_runner_up.so_what: It provides a formal and empirically broad way to quantify, predict, and reduce the hidden performance cost of coordination in LLM agent systems.
tech_runner_up.reason_not_higher: The framework appears limited to two-player cooperative settings and solo-tractable tasks; broader agent topologies, long-horizon environments, and deployment conditions may exhibit different coordination failures, while the proposed mitigation is only partial.

product.why_this_paper: Shows that LLM “is this neighborhood safe?” style advice can encode place-based demographic stigma even when names also carry real risk signal—changing how products should use LLMs for location/risk guidance.
product.decision_it_changes: Whether to ship LLM-generated location/safety/risk recommendations without place-name stigma audits, and how to trade off accuracy against demographic bias when neighborhood identity is an input.
product.action_for_reader: If any product surface uses LLMs for location, travel, housing, or local-risk guidance: run a name-vs-coordinates probe on your model for 20–50 places; require a bias review before launch; default to coordinates/features over evocative place names where possible.
product.talking_point: LLM urban-safety judgments can track neighborhood stigma attached to a name, not just measured risk.
product.caveat: Limited to two US cities and seven models; observational associations do not fully identify mechanisms or predict downstream harm in every deployment.
product.why_not_runner_up: Stronger immediate product/governance decision for consumer and enterprise location-advice surfaces than claim-level confidence calibration, which is powerful but more of an answer-UX control than a go/no-go on a whole class of LLM advice features.
product.title: Is Your Neighborhood Safe? Place-based Stigma in Large Language Models' Urban Safety Judgments
product.so_what: The study shows that LLM urban-safety advice can encode place-based demographic stigma even when neighborhood names also contain legitimate risk information, creating a consequential bias–accuracy tradeoff.
product.reason_not_higher: The analysis is limited to two US cities and seven models, and observational associations cannot fully identify the mechanisms behind models' judgments or predict downstream harm in real deployments.

product_runner_up.why_this_paper: Makes LLM confidence actionable at claim level so high-stakes products can route verification to uncertain statements instead of accepting/rejecting whole answers.
product_runner_up.decision_it_changes: How review/escalation UX is designed for LLM answers in decision-support products.
product_runner_up.action_for_reader: Prototype claim-level confidence on one high-stakes QA/decision flow; measure whether reviewers spend time on the uncertain claims rather than whole-response sampling.
product_runner_up.talking_point: A single response-level confidence score is too coarse when one answer mixes correct and incorrect claims.
product_runner_up.caveat: Evaluated primarily on factual QA; depends on reliable claim decomposition and manageable inference overhead in richer decision settings.
product_runner_up.title: Claim-Level Confidence Calibration for Reliable Decision Making with Large Language Models
product_runner_up.so_what: Claim-level calibration could make LLM-assisted decisions safer by directing verification or human review to specific uncertain statements rather than rejecting entire responses.
product_runner_up.reason_not_higher: The framework is evaluated primarily on factual QA, and its broader value depends on reliable claim decomposition, verification labels, and manageable inference-time overhead in more complex decision settings.
